continuation_reasoning:
merge sort, the list is divided into two halves, each half is sorted recursively, and then the two sorted halves are merged together. the process continues until the list is broken down into single elements, which are inherently sorted. the merging step combines two sorted lists into one sorted list by comparing the front elements of each list and appending the smaller one to the result.

merge sort is preferred over quicksort for linked lists because it has a guaranteed time complexity of o(n log n) in all cases, while quicksort can have a worst-case time complexity of o(n²). additionally, merge sort is more efficient for linked lists because it can merge two sorted linked lists in o(n) time without requiring random access, which is not efficient for linked lists. quicksort, on the other hand, relies on random access and partitioning, which is less efficient for linked lists.
